title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold \(r\in [0,1]\), decide whether \(v_{G}(s)>r\), where \(v_{G}(s)=\sup _{\sigma} \inf _{\tau} \Pr _{s}^{\sigma ,\tau}\)[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.

importance.reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.

progress.text: Condon establishes \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership for the stochastic-game decision problem and the foundational positional-strategy framework.
Ludwig gives a randomized subexponential algorithm requiring an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations.
Berthon, Katoen and Zhou publish a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games with binary probability encodings.
Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger present sound value iteration for stochastic games, including end components, with certified approximation bounds.
Baldan and coauthors extend fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. This convergence result does not give a general exact polynomial-time threshold decider.
Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang solve stopping binary SSGs on ladders in polynomial time; their introduction explicitly retains the general P question as open.

status_note: Rechecked on 11 September 2026. The inspected 2026 work on iteration and stopping ladder games does not give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for all exact threshold instances. No resolution was located in the later-work search.

context_blocks.text: This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\). That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies \(x=(x+x)/2\) for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability \(2^{- k}\), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only \(O(k)\) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\) operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

The exact branch formerly indexed as TCS-2427 asks for a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm returning optimal positional strategies for a finite, explicitly given, two-player zero-sum turn-based game. Each state is owned by one player; every available action has a rational reward to Max and a rational probability distribution over successor states. Min receives the opposite reward. A common rational discount multiplier \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) is part of the binary input, and Max's objective is \(\mathbb E[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t r_t]\). Multiplication by \(1-\gamma\) leaves optimal strategies unchanged. The factor is constant during a play but may approach one across inputs. Time must be polynomial in the complete encoding length, including \(\gamma\); polynomial dependence on \(1/(1-\gamma)\) alone is insufficient. Exact solving of this class and simple stochastic games are polynomial-time equivalent. The source's additional approximation branch has no precision selected here.

The 2023 source explicitly separates the known constant-discount algorithms from the input-dependent discount question. The checked 2024 paper invokes the reduction of discounted game values and optimal policies to SSGs. These connections motivate consolidating the exact branch into the present threshold problem; they do not establish that its polynomial-time target is solved.

sentences: A simple stochastic game combines choices of a maximizing player, choices of a minimizing player and fair random branching.
The project asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether the optimal probability of reaching a target exceeds a given rational threshold.
Optimal positional strategies provide short certificates, but finding them may require navigating exponentially many combinations.
Cycles also mean that solving local value equations without the correct reachability interpretation can give misleading answers.
Progress would clarify the computational cost of exact planning against both adversarial and random uncertainty.
